edition.locus: Against Marcion 1.12 (god without works = without cause = not God)

source_text: Ceterum et si esse eum possemus confiteri, sine causa esse eum deberemus argumentari . sine causa enim esset qui rem non haberet, quia res omnis causa est, ut sit aliquis, cuius res sit. porro in quantum nihil oportet esse sine causa, [id est sine re] quia si sine causa sit, proinde est atque si non sit. [non habens rei causam rem ipsam] in tantum deum dignius credam non esse quam esse sine causa. sine causa est enim qui rem non habendo non habet causam. deus autem sine causa, id est sine re, esse non debet. ita quotiens ostendo eum sine causa esse, tamquam sit, hoc constituo, non esse illum, quia si fuisset, omnino sine causa non fuisset. sic et ipsam fidem dico illum sine causa ab homine captare. aliter solito deum credere ex operum auctoritate formatum. quia nihil tale prospexit, per quod homo deum didicit. nam etsi credunt plerique in illum, non statim ratione credunt. non habentes dei pignus, opera eius deo digna. itaque hoc nomine cessationis et defectionis operum et impudentiae et malignitatis adfinis est: impudentiae, qua fidem non debitam sibi captat, cui praestruendae nihil prospexit. malignitatis. qua plures incredulitatis reos fecit, nihil fidei procurando.
pass_a_gloss: Sine re = sine causa = non deus. Fides sine operum pignore = impudentia/malignitas.
pass_b_english: For the rest, even if we could confess that he is, we ought to argue that he is without cause. For he would be without cause who had no thing, because every thing is a cause that someone be whose thing it is. Further, inasmuch as nothing ought to be without cause—[that is, without a thing]—because if it be without cause, it is just as if it be not—[not having the thing’s cause, the thing itself]—to that extent I will more worthily believe God not to be than to be without cause. For he is without cause who by not having a thing does not have a cause. But God ought not to be without cause, that is without a thing. So whenever I show him to be without cause, as if he were, I establish this—that he is not—because if he had been, he would not at all have been without cause.

So also I say that he captures faith itself from a human without cause—otherwise than is customary to believe God formed from the authority of works—because he has provided nothing such through which a human learned God. For even if very many believe in him, they do not at once believe with reason, not having God’s pledge, his works worthy of God. And so by this name of cessation and defect of works he is neighbor both to shamelessness and to malignity: to shamelessness, inasmuch as he captures faith not owed to himself, for constructing which he has provided nothing; to malignity, inasmuch as he has made more persons guilty of unbelief by procuring nothing for faith.
